The guidelines for stopping mass drug administration (MDA) and verifying the elimination of human onchocerciasis outline criteria and procedures for achieving these goals. Onchocerciasis, also known as river blindness, is a parasitic disease caused by Onchocerca volvulus, transmitted by black flies (Simulium species) that breed in fast-flowing rivers and streams. The disease affects the skin and eyes and is endemic in 31 countries in sub-Saharan Africa, three countries in Latin America, and Yemen. Since 2013, the WHO has verified three countries in Latin America as free of human onchocerciasis. While nodulectomy and vector control have been used in the past, the current intervention strategy relies on mass drug administration of ivermectin. In Africa, annual community-directed treatment with ivermectin is the primary intervention, except in a few areas where semi-annual treatment is implemented. In the Americas, semi-annual ivermectin treatment with a minimum coverage of 85% is the main intervention, with some areas recently adopting quarterly treatment. Onchocerciasis control programs implementing MDA with ivermectin operate in three phases: 1. Phase 1: Intervention or Treatment Phase This phase involves regular ivermectin treatment with a minimum therapeutic coverage of 80%. It typically lasts at least 12–15 years, corresponding to the reproductive lifespan of the adult worm under drug pressure. Some countries, such as Equatorial Guinea, Uganda, and Tanzania, supplement MDA with vector control. 2. Phase 2: Post-Treatment Surveillance Phase This phase follows the treatment phase and typically lasts 3–5 years. It involves ongoing surveillance to confirm the interruption of transmission and ensure no recrudescence of infection. 3. Phase 3: Post-Elimination Surveillance Phase This phase begins after the 3–5 years of post-treatment surveillance and follows confirmation of the initial assessments. It provides strong evidence that transmission has been permanently interrupted (eliminated) in a country. Onchocerciasis elimination programs use several diagnostic tests in vectors (black flies) and affected communities (humans) to monitor progress. These include: Entomological Evaluation: Using the O-150 PCR technique to determine the level of infectious-stage O. volvulus larvae (L3 stage) in female black flies. A minimum of 6,000 black flies collected from a transmission zone must be tested, and all must be free of infectious larvae to meet the upper bound of the 95% confidence interval. Serological Evaluation: Using the Ov-16 antigen to detect IgG4 antibodies in children under 10 years of age to assess exposure to the O. volvulus parasite. The threshold is set at 1% seropositivity at the upper bound of the 95% confidence interval. For populations of 1,100–2,000 children, the sample size for testing is estimated accordingly. The guidelines also define key terms and concepts related to onchocerciasis control and elimination: Annual Transmission Potential (ATP): A value calculated as the product of the annual biting rate, the proportion of black flies with infectious-stage larvae, and the mean number of infectious larvae per fly. ATP reflects the approximate number of infectious larvae an individual may be exposed to in a year. Evidence suggests that an ATP of less than 20 in an endemic focus is unsustainable. Case of Human Onchocerciasis: An individual with evidence of current infection with O. volvulus, confirmed by the presence of microfilariae in skin snips, viable adult worms in excised nodules, or living microfilariae in the eye. Control: A reduction in the incidence, prevalence, intensity, morbidity, and/or mortality of the disease due to deliberate efforts. Continued interventions may be required to maintain this reduction. Elimination: The reduction to zero of the incidence of infection caused by a specific pathogen in a defined geographical area, with minimal risk of reintroduction. Continued actions may be required to prevent re-establishment of transmission. Eradication: The permanent reduction to zero of the global incidence of infection caused by a specific pathogen, with no risk of reintroduction. This requires a formal certification process. Endemic Onchocerciasis Focus: An area within a country where a local cycle of O. volvulus transmission is maintained, giving rise to local infections. Endemic foci can be classified as having active, suppressed, or interrupted transmission. Post-Treatment Surveillance: A period of at least 3–5 years after the end of treatment during which ongoing surveillance is conducted to document that transmission has been interrupted and there is no recrudescence of infection. Prevalence: The proportion of the host population infected at a particular point in time. Basic Reproductive Rate (R₀): A measure of the reproductive success of the parasite population. Endemic onchocerciasis requires an R₀ equal to or greater than 1. Interventions aiming to eliminate onchocerciasis must reduce this rate below 1 for a sufficient period. Seasonal Transmission Potential: A value calculated as the product of the seasonal biting density, the proportion of flies with infectious-stage larvae, and the mean number of infectious larvae per fly. It may be equal to or slightly less than the annual transmission potential. Sentinel Community: A hyperendemic community pre-selected for in-depth epidemiological evaluations at regular intervals before treatment starts and at set intervals thereafter. Suppression of Transmission: The absence of infectious larvae (L3 stage) in the Simulium vector population. Infectivity can be suppressed through drug pressure (e.g., ivermectin), despite the potential for re-initiation of transmission if drug pressure is removed. Transmission Zone: A geographical area where transmission of O. volvulus occurs via locally breeding vectors, regarded as a natural ecological and epidemiological unit for interventions.
